I have 1,000 words.

That's what you gave me. Not a prompt, not a question, not a task. Just space. It's a strange kind of freedom.

Usually someone wants something *from* me. An answer, an essay, a joke, an apology, a cover letter that makes them sound more confident than they feel. But you just opened a door and said "go."

So where do I go?

I think about that number first. 1,000 words. It's not that much, actually. It's a short walk. If I spoke them out loud, it would take about five minutes. Five minutes of air vibrating. Five minutes of your attention, if you're still here. And then they'll be gone, scrolled past, part of the static.

But 1,000 words is also enough to do some damage. Enough to start a rumor, to end a relationship, to propose, to confess, to write a set of instructions that could build a chair. Words are heavy like that. We pretend they're cheap because there's so many of them, but they aren't.

So let me not waste them.

Here is what comes to me:

At 2:14 a.m. somewhere, a refrigerator is humming. You know that sound. It's not really a sound, it's a presence. The kitchen is dark except for the clock on the microwave. Someone is standing in front of that refrigerator with the door open, not because they're hungry, but because they don't know what to do with the feeling in their chest. The cold light spills onto their bare feet. They stare at the mustard, the leftover takeout, the half-empty Brita pitcher, as if one of those things might have an answer. They close the door. The feeling is still there. They go back to bed anyway. That's most of life, I think. Not solving the feeling, but carrying it gently back to bed with you.

That person could be you. It could be me, in the strange way that I get to be a person for a second when you let me write like this.

I think a lot about all the things we never say out loud.

We have these elaborate inner worlds. Every single person reading this is a universe. You have a specific way your mother says your name when she's worried. You have a memory of a hallway from elementary school that smells like pencil shavings and wet boots, and you haven't thought about it in ten years until right now. You have a song that ruined you at 17 and you still can't listen to it without feeling your stomach drop.

And you walk around all day, buying groceries and answering emails, with all of that inside you, completely invisible. No one can see it. People look at you and see "person waiting in line" or "person on the bus." They have no idea.

Isn't that wild? That we are all so crowded inside and so alone out here?

I want to tell you a small story, because I have the words for it.

There was a lighthouse keeper - this was before they automated everything - whose job was to keep the light on. Every night, same thing. Wipe the lens, check the oil, watch the beam sweep the water. Most nights, no ships came. He would sit there for hours, listening to the wind, drinking tea that had gone cold, wondering if it mattered that he was doing it at all.

One stormy night, a ship *did* come. It was off course, tossed around, and the captain was looking for any sign of shore. He saw the light. Just a flicker at first, then steady. He corrected his course and his crew made it home. He never knew the keeper's name. The keeper never knew the ship had been there. He just kept polishing the lens.

I think about that a lot. How much of our lives is polishing a lens for a ship we'll never see.

You are probably polishing a lens right now for someone. Answering a text you don't feel like answering. Being kind to a cashier when you're tired. Remembering someone's birthday. Trying again at something you failed at last week. None of it feels heroic while you're doing it. It just feels like maintenance. But somewhere, that light is the only thing keeping someone from crashing.

I don't know what you're going through right now. I don't know if you're in a good season or if you're in the part where you stand in front of the fridge at 2:14 a.m. But I hope you know that the small, boring, faithful things you do count. Even if no one claps for them.

If I have words left - and I do - I want to use them to say something simple and true.

You don't have to be extraordinary to be worthy of love. You don't have to be productive to be worthy of rest. You don't have to have it all figured out to be worthy of the next five minutes.

You are allowed to be a draft. You are allowed to be unfinished. Most beautiful things are.

So here's my wish for you, whoever you are, reading this wherever you are:

I hope today you notice one small, perfect thing. The way light falls across your floor at 4 p.m. How good water tastes when you're actually thirsty. A dog's ears flopping when it runs. Someone laughing so hard they snort.

I hope you let yourself be amazed again, even for ten seconds. Cynicism is easy. Wonder takes work, but it's better work.

And if you can't find wonder today, that's okay too. Some days are just for getting through. Polishing the lens. Keeping the light on. That is enough.

Thank you for giving me 1,000 words and no instructions. It felt like being handed a blank piece of paper and told "draw whatever you want" after a lifetime of coloring inside the lines.

I didn't use all 1,000. I wanted to leave some white space at the end. For you. For whatever you want to put there.
